passage:
Looking back, the word that fooled us was "custom". When Aman's family first came, his mother said, "We don't want anything, beta. Only your happiness." My parents cried with relief that their daughter had found a good family. Two weeks later, his aunt sent Papa a message: a "small list of what is usually given". A fridge, a washing machine, gold for six relatives, a car "of your choice", and a five-star wedding hall. No demand, she said. Just what everyone does.
I felt sick. Papa said we'd manage somehow. That night I called Jasleen, my friend from law school. She was quiet, then said, "Ritu, this is dowry. Calling it a gift doesn't change it. It's illegal." Hearing the word made it real.
The next day I told Aman directly. I said I would not marry into a family that sends lists. He was shocked, but he went to his parents himself. The list was withdrawn.

qa.q: What was on the list sent by Aman's aunt?
qa.a: A fridge, a washing machine, gold for six relatives, a car and a five-star wedding hall.

qa.q: How did Ritu feel when the list arrived?
qa.a: Ritu felt sick and uneasy, sensing the "custom" was really a demand.

qa.q: What was the first step that helped Ritu refuse?
qa.a: Recognising the list as dowry, with Jasleen naming it plainly, which gave Ritu the clarity to tell Aman she would not accept it.

qa.q: How might Ritu's Papa have felt when the list came?
qa.a: Papa was probably anxious and pressured, saying they would manage somehow because he feared losing a good match for his daughter.

grounding: It illustrates a bride's family told there is no demand, only custom, then receiving a list, and recognising it as dowry in order to refuse.

passage:
Harsha: Arnab, you awake? can't sleep
Arnab: yes. what's up
Harsha: found out today Appa has pledged the farm land for Divya's wedding
Harsha: the groom's side keeps saying "no demands" but then "people will expect a good function, some gold, a bike for him"
Arnab: that's a demand
Harsha: I know. Appa says if we give less they'll treat her badly after. Amma is scared no one else will marry her. she's 24!
Arnab: they love her. that's why they're this scared
Harsha: I'm angry and I can't even be angry at them
Arnab: when my sister got married we said no to everything. my uncles fought us. but three families in our street did the same after that
Harsha: really?
Arnab: really. someone has to go first
Harsha: I'll talk to Divya tomorrow. if she's ready, we both talk to Appa. and to the groom directly
Arnab: I'll come if you want
Harsha: thanks da

qa.q: What has Appa pledged for Divya's wedding?
qa.a: The farm land.

qa.q: Why are Harsha's parents willing to take such a risk?
qa.a: They are frightened and loving, fearing Divya will be treated badly or remain unmarried if they give less.

qa.q: What step is Harsha planning, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Talking to Divya first and then, together, to Appa and the groom directly; it respects Divya's wishes and challenges the demand openly.

qa.q: What does Arnab's family story suggest about change?
qa.a: It suggests that when one family refuses, others find courage, since three families on his street did the same afterwards.

grounding: It illustrates a bride's parents borrowing heavily out of fear and love, and how social change needs families to say no.

passage:
March: Four months after the wedding, Dilnaz's mother-in-law began to say it at every meal. "Your family sent such cheap steel. Our neighbour's bahu brought a car." Dilnaz, twenty-four, smiled and swallowed. Her husband said nothing.
May: The taunts became demands. "Ask your Abbu for two lakhs for the shop. It's the least he can do." When she refused, they stopped speaking to her for a week. She stopped calling her friends. She told herself it was normal, just how families are.
June: Her college friend Payal came to visit and noticed how thin and quiet Dilnaz was. In the café, Dilnaz finally told her everything. Payal held her hand. "This is harassment. It's not custom and it's not your fault." That afternoon, Payal sat with her while she called her Abbu and the women's helpline. The helpline connected her with a lawyer. Her father came to fetch her that evening.

qa.q: What did Dilnaz's mother-in-law demand in May?
qa.a: That Dilnaz ask her Abbu for two lakhs for the shop.

qa.q: How was Dilnaz feeling by May, and what shows it?
qa.a: She felt isolated and ashamed, stopping calls to friends and telling herself it was normal.

qa.q: What did Payal do that helped?
qa.a: She listened, named it as harassment and not Dilnaz's fault, and sat with her that same afternoon while she called her father and a helpline, which led to legal support.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz's Abbu have felt when she called?
qa.a: He was probably shocked and worried for his daughter, and protective enough to fetch her the same evening.

grounding: It illustrates a wife facing taunts and repeated demands after marriage, recognised as harassment, and help from trusted people and legal support.

passage:
Supervisor's note, accounts team, Friday.
Over the last two months Deepika has changed. She used to eat lunch with the team; now she eats at her desk. Her phone rings almost every hour, and she steps out to answer, coming back red-eyed. On Tuesday I overheard her say, "I'll ask Papa again, please don't shout." She flinches when anyone jokes about weddings.
I did not want to pry, so I asked her to join me for tea in the canteen. I said I'd noticed she seemed low and that she could tell me anything or nothing. After a long silence she said her in-laws keep asking why her family hasn't sent more. I listened without advising. I told her it was not her fault. I wrote the women's helpline number on a sticky note, and offered to sit with her if she wanted to call her sister. She kept the note. I will check in every day.
Zubin

qa.q: What did Deepika say on the phone on Tuesday?
qa.a: "I'll ask Papa again, please don't shout."

qa.q: What was Zubin feeling while noticing the changes in Deepika?
qa.a: Zubin felt worried and concerned, seeing her withdraw, flinch and return red-eyed, but careful not to pry.

qa.q: What did Zubin do that could matter greatly?
qa.a: Zubin listened without judgement, told Deepika it was not her fault, gave the helpline number, offered to sit with her while she called her sister, and planned to keep in daily contact.

qa.q: How might Deepika have experienced the tea with Zubin?
qa.a: She was probably scared and ashamed at first, then a little relieved to be listened to without being judged.

grounding: It illustrates a bystander at work who notices a woman withdrawn and pressured about money from her family, listens and points to help.

passage:
Ishita, you're angry about your cousin's in-laws and their demands? Good. Let your Shankar mama tell you about 1998. I was twenty-five, and my elder brother, your Periappa, was getting married. At the first planning meeting, my father said, "Of course the girl's side will give a scooter and gold." I felt my face go hot. I wanted to shout. But I waited until everyone had finished, and then I said, calmly, "Appa, if we take anything, it's dowry. I won't be part of that." The room went silent. My father was furious.
That night I sat with my Paati. She had been given away with a buffalo and a debt. She listened, then said, "The boy is right." The next morning she said it at breakfast, in front of everyone. Two uncles agreed. It took months, but Periappa's wedding happened with no scooter. Anger would have lost that fight. Calm, and Paati, won it.

qa.q: What did Shankar's father say the girl's side would give?
qa.a: A scooter and gold.

qa.q: How did young Shankar feel at the planning meeting, and how did he handle it?
qa.a: He felt angry, his face hot, but he waited and spoke calmly instead of shouting.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Shankar mama's story?
qa.a: Paati backing him at breakfast in front of everyone, which made two uncles agree and showed how one clear voice with an elder ally makes others braver.

qa.q: How might Paati have felt when young Shankar spoke to her?
qa.a: She probably felt moved and vindicated, remembering her own marriage with a buffalo and a debt.

grounding: It illustrates a relative who objects to dowry calmly at the planning stage and finds an ally among elders, making others braver.

passage: I'm Sangeeta, from the house next door. At the Sunday fair, little Pranav, five, stopped at a stall and hugged a pink doll with yellow hair. A man nearby laughed. "Doll? You're a boy!" Pranav's face crumpled. His mother knelt beside him. "Do you like her?" He nodded, eyes wet. "Then she can come home." Pranav carried the doll all the way back, singing to it.

qa.q: What did Pranav hug at the stall?
qa.a: A pink doll with yellow hair.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta have felt watching the man laugh?
qa.a: Sangeeta was probably uncomfortable and sorry for Pranav, noticing how his face crumpled.

qa.q: What did Pranav's mother do that helped?
qa.a: She stayed calm, asked what he liked and let him take the doll, so he did not learn to be ashamed of it.

qa.q: How did Pranav feel after his mother's answer?
qa.a: He went from ashamed and tearful to happy, singing to the doll on the way home.

grounding: It illustrates a parent who responds calmly when a boy wants a doll, while ridicule from a stranger shows how shame is taught.

passage: In the courtyard of their house near Sitapur, Sarika chachi called, "Sarita, come, roll the rotis." Sarita, ten, put down her book and went. Outside, her brother Mohan and the cousins were playing gilli-danda, shouting. Nobody called Mohan. Sarita rolled roti after roti, flour up to her elbows, and watched through the door. When the rotis were done, Mohan ran in first and was served first. Sarita said nothing. She just looked at her floury hands, then at his muddy ones. That night she asked Dadi, "Why does Mohan never roll?" Dadi paused, as if she had never been asked. "Hmm," she said. "Maybe tomorrow he will."

qa.q: What was Mohan playing?
qa.a: Gilli-danda, with the cousins.

qa.q: What was Sarita feeling as she watched Mohan through the door?
qa.a: She felt quietly hurt and aware something was unfair, though she said nothing.

qa.q: What could Sarika chachi do to make chores fair?
qa.a: She could call both Sarita and Mohan to help, and serve everyone together, so both children learn that work is shared.

qa.q: How might Dadi have seen Sarita's question?
qa.a: Dadi seemed surprised and thoughtful, as if she had never questioned who does the rolling before.

grounding: It illustrates a girl asked to help in the kitchen while her brother plays, who notices the unfairness before she can name it.

passage:
In Nairobi, Wanjiru, fifteen, had to be home by six-thirty, before dark. Her brother Kaito, sixteen, came home at nine from football, sometimes later. "It's for your safety," Mum said. Wanjiru stood in the kitchen, arms crossed. "So you trust him and not me?" Mum's face tightened. "It's not about trust. The road from the matatu stop is dark." "It's dark for Kaito too!" Kaito looked up from his phone. "She's got a point."
That Sunday they sat together at the table. Mum explained what actually worried her: the unlit road, the men who hung around the stage at night. Wanjiru listened. Then she suggested both of them share their location, both come home by seven-thirty on school nights, and whoever is later gets picked up by Dad. Mum thought, then nodded. Wanjiru felt heard for the first time. Kaito groaned about the new curfew, then laughed.

qa.q: What time did Wanjiru have to be home?
qa.a: By six-thirty, before dark.

qa.q: How did Wanjiru feel about the different curfews?
qa.a: She felt distrusted and resentful, asking whether Mum trusted Kaito and not her.

qa.q: What made the new rule fairer?
qa.a: They talked openly about the real risks, then set the same curfew, location sharing and a pickup plan for both children.

qa.q: How might Mum have felt when Wanjiru asked about trust?
qa.a: Mum probably felt hurt and defensive, because she saw the rule as protection, not distrust.

grounding: It illustrates a teenage girl with an earlier curfew than her brother who feels both protected and distrusted, and a fair rule reached by open talk.

passage:
Dear Sumit bhaiya,
I wanted to write this because I can't say it on the phone. When Dadaji died last month, I cried at the cremation, in front of everyone. Papa put his hand on my shoulder and said, "Be strong. Boys don't cry." One of the uncles laughed and said, "Look at him, like a girl." So I stopped. Since then I make jokes all the time. At school I got into a fight over nothing. Mummy says I've become "so rude". I don't know how to explain that it's all inside and has nowhere to go.
Then I remembered: at Dadaji's house, the night after, I saw you crying on the terrace. You didn't hide. You just said, "I miss him." That's the only time I felt normal.
Can I call you when it gets bad? I don't want to joke about everything anymore.
Darshan

qa.q: What did Papa say at the cremation?
qa.a: "Be strong. Boys don't cry."

qa.q: How has Darshan been feeling since the cremation?
qa.a: Darshan has been sad and angry inside, hiding grief behind jokes and even fighting at school.

qa.q: How can Sumit bhaiya support Darshan?
qa.a: He can say yes to calls, listen without mocking, and show again that missing someone and crying are normal.

qa.q: How might Papa see his words at the cremation?
qa.a: Papa probably thought he was helping Darshan be brave, without realising it taught him to hide his sadness.

grounding: It illustrates a boy told not to cry who hides sadness behind jokes and anger, and an older cousin whose honesty protects his feelings.

passage:
Vijay, your father wants you to be an engineer, and you want to cook? Let your Gargi athai tell you something. When I was twenty, I had topped my college in chemistry. My father said, "Do a B.Ed. Teaching is a good job for a girl. Easy hours, good for marriage." My twin brother, your father, wanted to paint. He was told, "Painting? You must earn. You're the son." So I became a teacher and he became an engineer. Both of us were pushed into moulds, one for a wedding, one for a salary.
The turning point came years later, when I told my father I wanted to do research after all. My mother, who had never spoken against him, said, "Let her." That changed everything. I got my PhD at thirty-two. Your father still paints on Sundays. Beta, talk to him. He knows that mould better than anyone.

qa.q: What did Gargi's father tell her to do after college?
qa.a: To do a B.Ed., because teaching was a good job for a girl.

qa.q: How might young Gargi have felt when told to choose teaching for marriage?
qa.a: She probably felt disappointed and boxed in, having topped her college in chemistry.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Her mother saying "Let her" when Gargi asked to do research; family support finally made a real choice possible.

qa.q: How might Gargi's twin brother have felt being told he must earn?
qa.a: He probably felt trapped and sad, giving up painting for engineering, which is why he still paints on Sundays.

grounding: It illustrates a young woman steered to an easy job for marriage while her brother is told to earn, and how real choice came with family support.
